title: Regulatory map
oneLiner: Know who holds each power, and how much legal force each layer of rules carries, before advising on anything.
overview: Banking supervision in Hong Kong sits with one statutory office. The Financial Secretary appoints the [[Monetary Authority]] under the Exchange Fund Ordinance (Cap. 66), and the [[HKMA]] is the organisation that supports the appointee. The Banking Ordinance (Cap. 155) gives banking powers to the MA personally: to authorize and revoke [[authorized institutions|authorized institution]], to supervise them and to issue guidelines. The MA's principal function is to promote the general stability and effective working of the banking system. Around the Ordinance sit three further layers. The first is binding rules on capital, liquidity, disclosure and exposure limits. The second is a large body of HKMA soft law, led by the [[Supervisory Policy Manual]]. The third is the industry [[Code of Banking Practice]]. Other regulators take over for particular activities: securities, insurance, personal data, deposit protection, dispute resolution and suspicious transaction reporting.

provisions.title: Appointment of the Monetary Authority
provisions.summary: The Financial Secretary must appoint a Monetary Authority. The appointee assists the FS on Exchange Fund matters and performs functions given by other Ordinances. The HKMA, set up on 1 April 1993, is the office that supports the MA.
provisions.counselNote: Banking powers belong to the MA personally. When you analyse where a decision came from and the limits of the power behind it, treat it as the MA's act under the relevant Ordinance.

provisions.title: Functions of the MA; power to issue guidelines
provisions.summary: Section 7(1) gives the MA the principal function of promoting the general stability and effective working of the banking system. Section 7(2) lists specific functions, including supervising compliance with the Ordinance, promoting proper standards of conduct and sound and prudent business practices, and taking reasonable steps to ensure AIs are operated in a responsible, honest and business-like manner. Section 7(3) lets the MA publish guidelines on how he proposes to exercise his functions.
provisions.counselNote: Statutory SPM modules are issued as guidelines under s.7(3) (CR-S-4 is one example), which is the legal basis for treating soft law as the standard the MA will apply. Check each module's classification line.

provisions.title: Grant of authorization; minimum criteria guideline
provisions.summary: The MA has a general discretion to grant or refuse authorization (s.16(1)), and must refuse if any Seventh Schedule criterion is not met (s.16(2)). Section 16(10) supports the MA's Guideline on Minimum Criteria for Authorization, which explains how he interprets those criteria.
provisions.counselNote: The criteria keep applying after authorization: the HKMA assesses compliance on a continuing basis and uses the same benchmarks to decide whether the bank keeps its licence. That is why a breach of a guideline carries licence-level risk.

provisions.title: Minimum criteria for authorization
provisions.counselNote: Treat the Schedule as the bank's permanent compliance specification. The HKMA ultimately frames every major issue (outsourcing failure, technology outage, mis-selling) as a question under these criteria.

provisions.title: Capital adequacy
provisions.summary: Sets out how AIs calculate their capital base and their risk-weighted amounts for credit, market and operational risk, and the minimum capital ratios. The Rules implement the Basel capital framework in Hong Kong.
provisions.counselNote: Capital treatment can decide whether a product, partnership or intra-group arrangement is commercially viable. Bring finance in early when structuring.

provisions.title: Liquidity requirements
provisions.summary: Apply the Basel III liquidity standards. Category 1 institutions must meet the Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio. Other AIs meet the Liquidity Maintenance Ratio and, where designated, a Core Funding Ratio.
provisions.counselNote: A digital bank's deposits are taken through an app and can move quickly. The bank's liquidity category and ratios shape product terms such as notice periods and promotional rates.

provisions.title: Large exposures and connected exposures
provisions.summary: Limit an AI's exposure to a single counterparty or a group of linked counterparties, and its exposure to connected parties.
provisions.counselNote: Many digital banks are owned by technology groups. Whenever the bank deals with its shareholder group, intra-group deposits, guarantees and service arrangements may count as connected exposures.

provisions.title: How the SPM works
provisions.summary: The SPM sets out the HKMA's supervisory policies, the minimum standards AIs are expected to attain in order to satisfy the requirements of the Banking Ordinance, and recommended best practice. Each module states its classification.
provisions.counselNote: Read IN first. Then index the modules that apply to the bank's business model. Minimum standards are mandatory in practice. Best practice is not, but the HKMA will use it in argument.

provisions.instrument: Code of Banking Practice (HKAB and DTC Association, endorsed by HKMA)
provisions.title: Industry conduct code for customer dealings
provisions.summary: A non-statutory code setting minimum standards for how AIs deal with customers. It covers matters such as disclosure of terms and charges, notice of changes, cards and electronic banking. AIs were to achieve full compliance with the revised provisions within six months, extended to 12 months for provisions requiring system changes.
provisions.counselNote: The Code is non-statutory, but the Guideline on Minimum Criteria for Authorization expects AIs to comply with it, and non-adherence can prompt a review of whether the bank still meets the authorization criteria. Treat gaps against the Code as regulatory issues.

provisions.title: Registration of AIs for SFC-regulated activities
provisions.summary: An AI that carries on regulated activities, such as dealing in or advising on securities, must be registered with the SFC as a registered institution. The HKMA is the front-line supervisor of that business.
provisions.counselNote: Investment, fund distribution and some digital-asset services sit in this dual regime. Staff doing the work must also be entered on the HKMA's register of relevant individuals.

checklist: Obtain the bank's authorization file: the licence, any conditions, the approval letters for controllers, chief executives and directors, and the correspondence on how the Digital Bank guideline was applied.
Build an obligations register that maps each applicable Cap. 155 provision, rule, SPM module, guideline and circular to an owner, a control and evidence.
Identify which SPM modules are statutory guidelines and which apply to the bank's business model, starting with governance, technology risk, operational resilience and outsourcing.
Set up a regulatory-change workflow: monitor the BRDR, HKMA circulars and SFC, IA and PCPD output, triage new items within a fixed time and record implementation deadlines.
Map every regulator touchpoint (HKMA case team, SFC, IA, PCPD, Deposit Protection Board, FDRC, JFIU), with notification duties and named contacts.
Confirm how the bank monitors its compliance with the Code of Banking Practice and how it evidences that compliance to the HKMA.
Adopt a research protocol: cite e-Legislation consolidated text using point-in-time versions, and keep a dated copy of every guideline version you rely on.
itAngle: Think of the rulebook as a dependency tree. The Ordinance and rules are the kernel. Statutory guidelines are mandatory configuration baselines. Circulars and FAQs are patches. An obligations register works best as a CMDB-style mapping from each requirement to a control, a system and evidence.

Pin versions. Modules and guidelines are revised in place, so record the date, version and BRDR document ID of anything you rely on. BRDR IDs begin with a date (e.g. 20231207-1-EN), but that date is not always the date printed on the document: SPM IN V.2 is dated 15 Nov 2024 yet carries ID 20241213-1-EN.
Statutory returns under s.63 are data pipelines. Data lineage and reconciliation controls are what make a return defensible if the MA questions it.

Conduct rules often become UI requirements. Examples are fee disclosures, notice of changes and the DPS membership sign, which has been required on electronic banking platforms since 1 January 2025. Build these into product release checklists.
virtualBankNotes: There is no separate statute for digital banks. Your bank is a licensed bank under Cap. 155 and is subject to the same Ordinance, rules and SPM. The Guideline on Authorization of Digital Banks sits on top; it was renamed from 'virtual banks' on 25 October 2024.

Some SPM modules carry extra weight for a digital bank: TM-G-1 (technology risk management), TM-E-1 (e-banking), OR-2 (operational resilience) and SA-2 (outsourcing). So do the HKMA's cyber-resilience circulars.
Use the current term 'digital bank' in policies and regulatory correspondence. Legacy documents and authorization papers may still say 'virtual bank'.
pitfalls: Treating guidelines as optional because they are 'not law'. The MA assesses the Seventh Schedule against them, and that is where the licence risk sits.
Reading the Ordinance alone. The prudential detail is in the Cap. 155 subsidiary rules, and the operative expectations are in SPM modules and circulars.
Relying on a stale PDF or a law-firm summary instead of the current BRDR version and the circular that issued it.
Forgetting dual regulation. A single in-app feature, such as a fund platform, can engage the HKMA, SFC standards, the PCPD and the Code at once.

glossary.definition: The statutory office appointed by the Financial Secretary under s.5A of the Exchange Fund Ordinance (MA). Banking powers under Cap. 155 are given to the MA personally.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the government organisation set up in 1993 to support the MA. In practice it is your counterpart in all supervisory dealings.
The term s.2 of Cap. 155 uses for any licensed bank, restricted licence bank or deposit-taking company (AI).
The HKMA's compendium of supervisory policies, minimum standards and best practice for AIs (SPM), organised by subject into coded modules.
A guideline or SPM module issued under a statutory power, usually s.7(3) of Cap. 155. It creates no offence, but it is the benchmark the MA applies when assessing the authorization criteria.
The Banking Regulatory Document Repository: the HKMA's online library of guidelines, circulars, SPM modules and the Guide to Authorization, launched in March 2025.
An AI registered with the SFC under s.119 SFO to carry on regulated activities such as dealing in or advising on securities. The HKMA supervises it front-line.
A non-statutory code issued by HKAB and the DTC Association and endorsed by the HKMA. It sets minimum standards for how AIs deal with customers.

title: Perimeter & licence tiers
oneLiner: Defines your bank's exclusive franchise and the edges where partners, affiliates and new products can breach it.
overview: Hong Kong licenses activities, not business models. The Banking Ordinance reserves two activities. Only a bank may carry on [[banking business]] (s.11). Taking [[deposits|deposit]] as a business needs some form of authorization (s.12). Authorized institutions sit in three tiers: licensed banks, [[restricted licence banks|restricted licence bank]] and [[deposit-taking companies|deposit-taking company]]. What separates the tiers is mainly which deposits each may take. Your employer is a licensed bank, authorized under the HKMA's guideline for a [[digital bank]], so it holds the full deposit-taking franchise. The perimeter also works outward. It decides who may call itself a bank, who may advertise for deposits, and which neighbouring activities need their own licences: stored value, lending, remittance, stablecoins, securities and insurance. A 2026 Bill would merge the bottom two tiers.
deepDive:
Section 11 reserves 'banking business' (s.2) to banks: in essence, current, savings and similar accounts repayable on demand or within less than three months, and cheque services. Section 12 is wider: any business of taking deposits needs authorization, subject to the s.3(1) exemptions and the exclusions from 'deposit'. 'Business' means systematic, repeated activity, and s.12(8) presumes a business where deposits are taken on five or more occasions within any 30 days, absent evidence to the contrary. For a novel product, test each limb: a loan of money, any exemption or exclusion, and business.

The tiers:
- A licensed bank alone may operate current and savings accounts and take deposits of any size and maturity.
- A restricted licence bank (RLB) may take deposits of HK$500,000 or more, of any maturity.
- A deposit-taking company (DTC) may take deposits of HK$100,000 or more with an original term of at least three months.

Minimum capital is HK$300 million for a locally incorporated licensed bank, HK$100 million for an RLB and HK$25 million for a DTC. Overseas banks may operate as branches; a DTC must be locally incorporated. A Bill gazetted on 5 June 2026 would merge DTCs into the RLB tier after a five-year transition; check its status and commencement before relying on dates.

A digital bank holds no separate type of licence. The HKMA's guideline (revised May 2018, renamed October 2024) applies the Seventh Schedule to banks operating mainly through electronic channels. It requires local incorporation, a Hong Kong intermediate holding company where the owner is not a bank or financial institution, a physical presence in Hong Kong and an exit plan. Eight licences were granted in 2019.

Section 97 bars non-banks from using 'bank' without the MA's consent, and the HKMA treats domain names and logos as covered. Section 92 prohibits deposit advertisements unless an exception applies, chiefly for deposits with an AI; under the MA's s.92(6) guideline (May 2002), offshore internet material is caught if targeted at the Hong Kong public.

Neighbouring regimes: a licensed bank is a deemed licensee for [[stored value facility]] business under Cap. 584; money lender and money service operator licensing do not apply to AIs; issuing a [[fiat-referenced stablecoin]] needs a separate Cap. 656 licence; securities business needs SFC registration and insurance distribution needs IA licensing.

provisions.title: Prohibition on banking business except by a bank
provisions.summary: Only a bank authorized under the Ordinance (a licensed bank) may carry on banking business in Hong Kong. Contravention is an offence.
provisions.counselNote: This section defines your bank's exclusive franchise: current and savings accounts and cheque services. Partners and affiliates that offer account-like features must not cross into it.

provisions.title: Prohibition on taking deposits as a business
provisions.summary: Only an authorized institution of some tier may carry on a business of taking deposits (s.12(1)). Section 3(1) lists categories of persons not subject to the restriction. Section 12(8) presumes a business where a person took deposits on at least five separate occasions within any 30 days, absent evidence to the contrary.
provisions.counselNote: Apply this test to fintech partners, group e-wallets and 'savings' features run by non-bank affiliates. If customer money is taken as a loan repayable to the customer and the activity is a business, it has to sit inside the bank.

provisions.title: Key definitions
provisions.summary: Section 2 defines 'banking business', 'deposit' (with exclusions) and 'authorized institution', among others. 'Banking business' means receiving money from the general public on current, deposit, savings or similar accounts repayable on demand or within less than three months (or at call or on notice of less than that period), or paying or collecting cheques drawn by or paid in by customers. 'Deposit' means a loan of money at interest, at no interest or at negative interest, or repayable at a premium or with other consideration, subject to listed exclusions.
provisions.counselNote: Start every perimeter opinion here. The exclusions from 'deposit' decide whether prepaid balances, collateral and intra-group funding are caught.

provisions.title: Restriction on use of 'bank'
provisions.summary: Without the MA's written consent, a non-bank may not use 'bank', its derivatives or the Chinese equivalent in its business name, or represent that it is a bank. HKMA guidance treats domain names and logos as covered. There are limited exemptions, for example for local representative offices of overseas banks (s.97(1A)).
provisions.counselNote: Check group companies, app names, domains and social media handles. The HKMA publicly warns about crypto and other firms that misuse 'bank'.

provisions.title: Deposit advertisements
provisions.summary: Section 92 prohibits issuing advertisements or documents that invite the public to make deposits, unless an exception applies. The main exception is material about deposits with an AI. Advertisements for deposits to be placed outside Hong Kong must meet the Fifth Schedule disclosure requirements. Under a guideline issued under s.92(6) in May 2002, the MA treats offshore internet material as caught where it is targeted at the Hong Kong public.
provisions.counselNote: Your own advertisements fall within the exception. Co-branded, affiliate and influencer campaigns must clearly promote the bank's deposits, and they must also comply with the Code of Banking Practice.

provisions.instrument: Guideline on Authorization of Digital Banks (formerly Virtual Banks)
provisions.title: Authorization criteria applied to digital banks
provisions.counselNote: This is your licence-specific rulebook. In practice the HKMA monitors the commitments made at authorization (business plan, exit plan, ownership) as continuing obligations.

provisions.instrument: Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance (Cap. 584)
provisions.title: Stored value facilities
provisions.summary: Issuing a multi-purpose stored value facility requires a licence from the MA. Licensed banks are treated as deemed licensees, and SVF business run by banks is subject to the same supervision as non-bank licensees.
provisions.counselNote: A wallet-style or prepaid feature may be an SVF rather than a deposit. The classification changes the rules that apply and the customer protection available.

provisions.title: Licensing of stablecoin issuers
provisions.summary: Creates an HKMA licensing regime for issuers of fiat-referenced stablecoins. The first licences were granted on 10 April 2026 to The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited and Anchorpoint Financial Limited.
provisions.counselNote: A banking licence does not authorize stablecoin issuance; HSBC needed a separate licence. Analyse stablecoin projects separately from tokenised deposits, which remain bank deposits.

provisions.title: Moving from three tiers to two, and other Banking Ordinance reforms
provisions.summary: The Bill amends the Banking Ordinance in five areas: regulation of bank holding companies, engagement of skilled persons for supervisory purposes, modernisation of enforcement provisions, simplification of the three-tier system into two tiers, and technical amendments. Existing DTCs would have five years to become RLBs or wind down their deposit-taking. It also amends the Hong Kong Association of Banks Ordinance and the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance, and was scheduled for First and Second Reading in LegCo on 17 June 2026.
provisions.counselNote: The tier merger barely touches a licensed bank's own franchise, but the holding-company, skilled-person and enforcement changes are likely to matter, especially for a bank held through an intermediate holding company. Confirm the enacted text and commencement provisions before relying on them.

checklist: Inventory every product and feature, and record which licence or exemption each relies on: banking licence, SVF deemed licence, SFC registration, IA licence or none.
Review group companies, partners and affiliates for any activity that could amount to taking deposits as a business. Bring such activity into the bank or restructure it.
Audit every use of 'bank' across group entity names, domains, app-store listings and social media handles. Obtain the MA's consent or rename where needed.
Clear deposit marketing against s.92 and the Code of Banking Practice, including co-branded, affiliate and influencer content.
Keep the commitments made at authorization (business plan, exit plan, ownership structure) current, and engage the HKMA before any material change.
Before any stablecoin, tokenised deposit or digital-asset design is fixed, analyse it against Cap. 656, the SFC regime and Cap. 155, and engage the HKMA early.
Track the Banking Legislation (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill 2026 to enactment and diarise its commencement dates.
itAngle: Encode licence limits as hard constraints in the product catalogue and core banking configuration, much like authorization scopes on an API. A misconfigured product or feature flag can itself be a perimeter breach.

Brand-protection tooling (domain and app-store monitoring, typosquat detection) also gathers intelligence for s.97 enforcement. The HKMA publishes alerts on fraudulent bank websites and on firms that misuse 'bank'.
Whether offshore internet material is 'targeted at' Hong Kong is judged on the factors in the MA's s.92(6) guideline. Ad-tech configuration, geo-targeting settings and logs are your evidence.
Test the exit plan as you would a disaster-recovery plan, with runbooks covering extraction of depositor data, the repayment channels and how repayment is funded.
virtualBankNotes: The eight digital banks licensed in 2019 all hold full banking licences. They may run current and savings accounts, take deposits of any size and maturity, and are members of the Deposit Protection Scheme.

The guideline requires local incorporation. A parent that is not a bank or financial institution must hold the bank through a Hong Kong intermediate holding company, and the HKMA can attach supervisory conditions to that company.

The 2018 guideline expected no minimum-balance requirements or low-balance fees. It also required an exit plan setting out the triggers, who may activate it, the repayment channels and the funding. Check the current 2024 wording of both points.
Ownership by a technology group creates perimeter risk at the edges. The parent's wallet, lending or wealth apps must not take deposits or present themselves as the bank.
pitfalls: Assuming 'deposit' means only bank accounts. Prepaid balances, customer float and 'savings pots' in non-bank apps can be deposits unless an exclusion applies.
Assuming the banking licence covers everything. Stablecoin issuance, securities business and insurance distribution each need their own licence or registration.
Letting group or partner branding use 'bank' in names, domains or app listings without the MA's consent.
Describing the three-tier structure without noting the pending move to two tiers, or quoting commencement dates for it before the enacted text confirms them.

glossary.definition: Defined in s.2 of Cap. 155. It means receiving money from the general public on current, deposit, savings or similar accounts repayable on demand or within less than three months (or at call or on notice of less than that period), or paying or collecting cheques drawn by or paid in by customers. Only licensed banks may carry it on.

Defined in s.2 of Cap. 155 as a loan of money at interest, at no interest or at negative interest, or repayable at a premium or with other consideration, subject to a list of exclusions. Taking deposits as a business requires authorization.
The second-tier AI. It may take deposits of HK$500,000 or more of any maturity but may not operate current or savings accounts. It has traditionally been used for merchant and investment banking.
The third-tier AI. It may take deposits of HK$100,000 or more with an original maturity of at least three months. Under the 2026 Bill the tier would be merged into the restricted licence bank tier.

The HKMA's term since October 2024, replacing 'virtual bank', for a bank that delivers services mainly or only through the internet or other electronic channels. It is a licensed bank, not a separate type of licence.

A facility that stores value paid in advance, which can be used to pay for goods and services or transferred to others. It is regulated under Cap. 584, and licensed banks are treated as deemed licensees.
A crypto-asset designed to hold a stable value by reference to one or more official currencies. Issuing one within the scope of Cap. 656 requires an HKMA licence.

title: Authorization
oneLiner: The licence is conditional and continuing: lose any minimum criterion and the bank faces suspension or revocation.
overview: In Hong Kong only an [[authorized institution]] may take deposits from the public, and only a licensed bank may carry on banking business in the full sense. Authorization is granted by the [[Monetary Authority]] within what is currently a [[three-tier banking system]] of licensed banks, restricted licence banks and deposit-taking companies. Your employer is a licensed bank that is also a [[digital bank]], the HKMA's term since October 2024 for what were called virtual banks. The gate is the [[Seventh Schedule]] to the Banking Ordinance: minimum criteria covering fit and proper people, capital, liquidity, systems of control, prudent conduct and minimum paid-up capital. It is less a one-off exam than a health check the bank must keep passing, because ceasing to meet the criteria is a ground for suspension or revocation. Digital banks meet the same criteria, read through a dedicated HKMA guideline.
deepDive:
Mechanics. An application is made to the MA (s.15), which grants or refuses it under s.16 and may attach conditions. Under s.16(10) the MA publishes how it reads the Seventh Schedule: the Guideline on Minimum Criteria for Authorization (re-issued February 2026) and, for your bank, the Guideline on Authorization of Digital Banks (October 2024), reproduced in Chapter 9 of the Guide to Authorization. These guidelines are not law, but they are how the MA decides whether it is satisfied, so treat them as the licence's terms of reference.

What the criteria demand. The Schedule is outcome-based: fit and proper chief executives, directors and controllers; adequate capital and liquidity (calibrated through the Banking (Capital) Rules and Banking (Liquidity) Rules); adequate provisioning; adequate accounting systems and systems of control; business conducted with integrity, prudence and professional competence; and minimum paid-up share capital of HK$300 million for a licensed bank. The digital bank guideline applies the same floor.

The digital-bank overlay. Expect to evidence: local incorporation and a physical presence in Hong Kong; where the bank is not majority-owned by a supervised bank or financial institution, a Hong Kong [[intermediate holding company]] subject to supervisory conditions; letters of comfort from controllers; a credible business plan with no minimum-balance requirements or low-balance fees; technology risk management to [[Supervisory Policy Manual]] standards, tested by independent expert assessments (one with the application, a more detailed one before launch); and an [[exit plan]] for an orderly, solvent unwind.

Keeping the licence. Eighth Schedule grounds include, in substance, ceasing to meet the criteria, breaching conditions or the Ordinance, and threats to depositors' interests. After consulting the Financial Secretary, the MA can propose revocation (s.22), giving notice of the grounds and an opportunity to be heard, or suspend authorization, temporarily in urgent cases (s.24) or for a longer period (s.25). Appeals lie to the Chief Executive in Council (s.132A). In practice the HKMA escalates through supervisory dialogue, conditions and s.52 powers long before revocation.

Watch list. The Banking Legislation (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill 2026, gazetted on 5 June 2026, would merge the lower two tiers into a two-tier system and give the MA direct powers over designated bank holding companies; most provisions are proposed to commence on 1 January 2027 if enacted.

provisions.title: Grant of authorization, conditions and interpretive guidelines
provisions.summary: The MA may grant or refuse authorization as a bank, restricted licence bank or deposit-taking company and may attach conditions; grant turns on the MA being satisfied that the Seventh Schedule criteria are met. Section 16(10) empowers the MA to publish guidelines on how it interprets those criteria.
provisions.counselNote: Your licence conditions are bespoke, binding and often sit in correspondence rather than the statute; keep them in a tracked register alongside the s.16(10) guidelines.

provisions.title: Minimum criteria for authorization
provisions.summary: Sets the criteria an institution must meet: fit and proper chief executives, directors and controllers; adequate capital, liquidity and provisions; adequate accounting systems and systems of control; business conducted with integrity, prudence and professional competence; and minimum paid-up share capital (HK$300 million for a licensed bank, raised from HK$150 million by a 2002 amendment).
provisions.counselNote: The criteria apply continuously, not only at grant; use the Schedule as the master framework against which board papers, launches and incidents are tested.

provisions.instrument: Guideline on Authorization of Digital Banks
provisions.ref: 25 Oct 2024 (issued under s.16(10); replaced the 2018 Guideline on Authorization of Virtual Banks)
provisions.title: How the minimum criteria apply to digital banks
provisions.summary: Explains how the Seventh Schedule applies to banks that deliver services mainly through electronic channels: local incorporation, physical presence in Hong Kong, ownership expectations (including a Hong Kong intermediate holding company where the bank is not majority-owned by a supervised bank or financial institution), the HK$300 million capital floor, a credible business plan without minimum balances or low-balance fees, technology risk management backed by independent expert assessment, outsourcing, customer protection and an exit plan.
provisions.counselNote: This is the document the HKMA will hold your bank to; update internal policies and contracts that still cite the superseded virtual bank guideline.

provisions.instrument: HKMA Guideline on Minimum Criteria for Authorization
provisions.title: HKMA interpretation of each minimum criterion
provisions.summary: Sets out how the MA interprets each Seventh Schedule criterion, including the fit and proper considerations for directors, chief executives and controllers. The February 2026 re-issue reportedly focused on resolution-related expectations, such as maintaining liquidity, funding and operational capabilities that support an orderly resolution.
provisions.counselNote: Read it before any appointment, shareholder change or material business change; it is the practical rulebook behind most HKMA approvals.

provisions.title: Authorization of digital banks (consolidated restatement)
provisions.summary: Reproduces the digital bank guideline within the HKMA's Guide to Authorization and states that it may include updated information not yet reflected in the guideline itself. The HKMA also points prospective applicants to Chapters 2, 4 and 8 of the Guide.
provisions.counselNote: Check Chapter 9 as well as the 2024 guideline, since it may carry newer cross-references.

provisions.title: Application for authorization
provisions.summary: Applications for authorization are made to the MA, supported by the information and documents the MA requires.
provisions.counselNote: Statements in the application (business plan, IT architecture, exit plan) become the baseline the HKMA supervises against; material departures later should be discussed with the HKMA first.

provisions.title: Revocation of authorization and the grounds for it
provisions.summary: The MA, after consulting the Financial Secretary, may propose to revoke an authorization where a ground in the Eighth Schedule exists. The institution must be told the grounds and given an opportunity to be heard, and the effective date is fixed only once appeal rights are exhausted or waived. The grounds include, in substance, ceasing to meet the minimum criteria, contravening the Ordinance or conditions, and circumstances threatening depositors' interests.
provisions.counselNote: Every Seventh Schedule weakness is a potential Eighth Schedule ground; escalation logic in your compliance framework should reflect that.

provisions.title: Temporary suspension and suspension of authorization
provisions.summary: Part VI allows the MA, after consulting the Financial Secretary, to suspend authorization on the same grounds as revocation: temporarily under s.24 (an urgent route, reported as up to 14 days) or for a longer period under s.25 (reported as up to six months, renewable). Secondary sources indicate that a suspended institution may not carry on deposit-taking business while suspended.
provisions.counselNote: Suspension is the realistic severe outcome for a distressed bank; your crisis playbook should cover the notice and representation process and depositor communications.

provisions.title: Appeals against MA decisions
provisions.summary: Specified decisions of the MA, including a proposed revocation of authorization, may be appealed to the Chief Executive in Council.
provisions.counselNote: Know the appeal route and timetable before a contentious HKMA decision arrives, not after.

provisions.title: Licence fees
provisions.summary: Prescribes the fees payable on authorization and on renewal at each anniversary of the authorization date. The banking licence and renewal fee has been HK$610,000 since 12 June 2024; on 17 June 2026 the Government gave notice of a resolution, to be moved in LegCo on 8 July 2026, to raise it to HK$750,000.
provisions.counselNote: Diary the anniversary date and confirm the current amount; fees are amended by LegCo resolution, not by HKMA circular.

checklist: Build a criteria map linking each Seventh Schedule criterion and each digital bank guideline expectation to an owner, evidence, board reporting line and last test date.
Extract every condition in the authorization letter and later variations into a tracked obligations register with triggers and owners.

Diary the licence fee renewal (the authorization anniversary), confirm whether the fee resolution moved on 8 July 2026 was passed, and track the Banking Legislation (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill 2026 through LegCo.
Confirm that controllers' letters of comfort remain in force and reassess them whenever a parent's financial position or ownership changes.
Review the exit plan at least annually and after any business-model change, and test its operational steps rather than leaving it as a document.
Discuss material changes to the business plan, core platforms, outsourcing or target segments with the HKMA before implementation.
Prepare a suspension and revocation playbook covering Eighth Schedule triggers, the notice and representation process, the s.132A appeal route and depositor communications.
Keep the independent IT assessment reports and evidence of remediation of every finding ready for supervisory review.
itAngle: Treat the Seventh Schedule like a control framework: map each criterion to control objectives and evidence, much as you would map ISO 27001 controls into a statement of applicability. The HKMA asks for evidence, not policy documents.

The adequate accounting systems and systems of control criterion is where IT bites hardest: core banking, general ledger and regulatory reporting pipelines must be reliable, because HKMA returns are only as good as the data lineage behind them.

The independent expert IT assessments are in effect architecture and security audits at two gates, design (with the application) and pre-production (before launch); run them with severity-rated findings, owners and closure evidence, measured against the HKMA's technology risk modules (notably TM-G-1).

An exit plan is a decommissioning runbook: it needs customer data export formats, notification channels, payment-scheme offboarding, vendor termination sequencing and tested deposit repayment processes.
virtualBankNotes: Since 25 October 2024 the HKMA uses the term digital bank, and the Guideline on Authorization of Digital Banks superseded the 2018 virtual bank guideline; the authorization test is still the Seventh Schedule.
A digital bank is a licensed bank: the same Ordinance, Seventh Schedule, HK$300 million capital floor and SPM apply. The guideline adds expectations rather than exemptions.
No minimum balance requirements or low-balance fees: a pricing constraint that counsel should police through product approval.

The HKMA's August 2024 review found the eight digital banks had met the policy objectives but none was profitable at end-2023, and saw no strong justification for new licences at that time; expect continued scrutiny of business plan viability.
pitfalls: Treating authorization as a closing event: the criteria are continuing, and drifting below any of them is a revocation or suspension ground.
Overlooking bespoke licence conditions, which are often more specific than the statute and live in HKMA correspondence.
Citing the superseded 2018 virtual bank guideline or outdated terminology in policies, submissions and contracts.
Changing the business model (new segments, outsourcing, products) without revisiting the business plan and exit plan the HKMA relied on.

glossary.definition: The statutory office, held by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, that exercises the powers under the Banking Ordinance, including authorization, approvals and revocation.
A bank, restricted licence bank or deposit-taking company authorized under the Banking Ordinance. Only authorized institutions may take deposits from the public in Hong Kong.

Hong Kong's current structure of licensed banks (full banking business, including current and savings accounts), restricted licence banks and deposit-taking companies, the latter two being limited in the deposits they may take. A 2026 Bill proposes merging deposit-taking companies into the restricted licence bank tier to create a two-tier system.
The schedule to the Banking Ordinance listing the minimum criteria for authorization, which must be met at grant and continuously afterwards.

The HKMA's term since October 2024 (formerly virtual bank) for a bank that delivers services primarily, if not entirely, through the internet or other electronic channels rather than physical branches.
A Hong Kong-incorporated holding company between a digital bank and owners that are not supervised banks or financial institutions, on which the HKMA imposes supervisory conditions.
A plan, required of digital bank applicants, for unwinding the business in an orderly and solvent manner if the business model fails.
The HKMA's collection of supervisory modules (such as CG-1 and TM-G-1). Many are statutory guidelines issued under s.7(3) of the Banking Ordinance; others are non-statutory guidance notes.

title: Controllers & key people
oneLiner: Owners, directors and senior managers need prior HKMA approval or notification; group deals and appointments fail without it.
overview: The Banking Ordinance regulates who may own and who may run a bank, not only what the bank does. Before anyone becomes a [[minority shareholder controller]], [[majority shareholder controller]] or [[indirect controller]] of a Hong Kong-incorporated bank, the Monetary Authority must consent. Chief executives, their alternates and directors also need the MA's prior approval, and senior [[managers|manager]] must be notified to it. Around this statutory core the HKMA has layered governance expectations: a board with a real [[independent non-executive directors|INED]] element, pay that does not reward reckless risk-taking, a bank culture programme, and reference checks so misconduct does not follow people from bank to bank. For a digital bank owned by a technology or fintech group, this area also covers how the parent stands behind the bank and how intra-group dealings are controlled.
deepDive:
Controllers. Section 70 prohibits becoming a controller of a locally incorporated AI without the MA's prior written consent. The thresholds come from the s.2 definitions: 10% or more of voting power (minority), more than 50% (majority), or influence over directors who are accustomed to act on a person's instructions (indirect). Voting power is counted with associates and through holding companies, so a restructuring of a tech parent, a new fund investor or a parent-level IPO can trigger consent even though the bank's own register is unchanged. Consent can be conditional: today the HKMA reaches holding companies indirectly, through conditions attached to their s.70 consent, and the Banking Legislation (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill 2026 would add direct powers over designated holding companies. Section 70A lets the MA object to existing controllers. Treat s.70 consent as a condition precedent in every deal touching the group cap table, and expect the HKMA to ask new controllers for a [[letter of comfort]].

People. Section 71 requires MA consent before a person becomes chief executive, alternate chief executive or (for a locally incorporated AI) director. Managers are notified under s.72B rather than approved, but the fit and proper approach in the Guideline on Minimum Criteria for Authorization applies to them in substance. If the bank is a registered institution for securities business, the HKMA's October 2017 accountability circular, its counterpart to the SFC's [[Manager-in-Charge]] regime, expects it to identify the senior individuals principally responsible for each regulated-activity business and function; executive officers also need MA consent (s.71C).

Governance and culture. CG-1 (V.4, August 2025) sets board, INED, committee and conflicts expectations; CG-5, a guidance note, governs remuneration; the March 2017 Bank Culture Reform circular makes the board own culture. The [[Mandatory Reference Checking Scheme]], widened in Phase 2 from 30 September 2025, requires conduct references covering up to seven years; build it into HR workflows.

Group dealings. Exposures to connected parties, including the parent group, controllers and directors, are limited under Part 8 of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules, with systems expectations in CR-G-9. For a tech-parented digital bank, intra-group cloud, data, marketing and payment arrangements need arm's-length terms, outsourcing controls and exposure monitoring.

provisions.title: MA consent to become a controller
provisions.summary: No person may become a minority shareholder controller (10% to 50% of voting power), majority shareholder controller (over 50%) or indirect controller of an AI incorporated in Hong Kong without the MA's prior written consent, which may be given subject to conditions. The requirement does not apply to controllers of AIs incorporated outside Hong Kong.
provisions.counselNote: Upstream changes in a tech parent's ownership can create a new controller of the bank; run a s.70 analysis on every group-level transaction and build HKMA review time into deal timetables.

provisions.title: Objection to existing controllers
provisions.summary: Empowers the MA to object to a person who is already a controller, for example where that person is no longer fit and proper, with statutory consequences for the controller's position. A 2001 amendment also enabled the MA to impose conditions on existing controllers.
provisions.counselNote: Controller approval is not a once-only pass; sanctions, enforcement action or insolvency at a parent should prompt a fresh assessment and early HKMA dialogue.

provisions.title: Approval of chief executives and directors
provisions.summary: No person may become the chief executive (or alternate chief executive) of an AI, or a director of an AI incorporated in Hong Kong, without the MA's written consent. The MA may withdraw consent if it ceases to be satisfied that the person is fit and proper.
provisions.counselNote: Make MA consent a condition of every board appointment and succession plan; an appointment that takes effect before consent is a breach.

provisions.title: Notification of managers
provisions.summary: An AI must notify the MA of the individuals it appoints as managers, that is, persons principally responsible (alone or jointly) for the conduct of particular affairs or business of the institution. The regime, added in 2001, is linked to the businesses and functions listed in the Fourteenth Schedule.
provisions.counselNote: Decide deliberately who is a s.72B manager (heads of technology, risk, compliance, AML and so on); the list drives MRC coverage and accountability mapping.

provisions.title: Corporate governance of locally incorporated AIs
provisions.summary: Statutory guideline under s.7(3) setting expectations on board responsibilities, structure and composition, the chair, INEDs, board committees, appointment of directors (fit and proper, commitment, succession) and conflicts of interest. The HKMA said the 2025 updates were primarily to align with international standards.
provisions.counselNote: Benchmark board and committee charters, INED numbers and expertise, and directors' time commitments against CG-1, and document the rationale for any departure.

provisions.title: Guideline on a Sound Remuneration System
provisions.summary: Guidance note requiring remuneration systems consistent with effective risk management, covering board oversight, pay structure, risk-adjusted performance measurement, alignment with risk time horizons, and remuneration disclosure. The 2021 revision reflected Financial Stability Board guidance on using remuneration tools to address misconduct risk.
provisions.counselNote: Growth-stage digital banks tend to reward customer acquisition; make sure sales metrics do not dominate variable pay and that malus and clawback tools can respond to misconduct.

provisions.title: Bank Culture Reform
provisions.summary: Asks locally incorporated AIs to strengthen governance, incentive systems, and assessment and feedback mechanisms to promote sound culture, with the board setting the tone. A December 2018 circular added self-assessments, focused reviews and culture dialogues.
provisions.counselNote: Expect the HKMA to test culture through outcomes such as complaints, incidents and staff surveys; give the board evidence, not slogans.

provisions.title: Management accountability at registered institutions
provisions.summary: For AIs registered with the SFC to carry on regulated activities, treats chief executives (including alternates), s.71 directors, s.72B managers and s.71C executive officers as management, and required each institution to identify the individuals principally responsible for its regulated-activity businesses and functions, with an organisation chart, by 16 April 2018.
provisions.counselNote: Relevant if the bank distributes investment products or carries on other regulated activities; keep the accountability map consistent with s.72B notifications.

provisions.instrument: Mandatory Reference Checking Scheme (HKAB/DTCA guidelines, endorsed by HKMA)
provisions.title: Conduct-related reference checks
provisions.summary: AIs hiring into covered roles must request conduct-related information from current and former employers covering up to seven years, and must respond to such requests. Phase 1 covered senior roles such as directors, chief executives and notified managers; Phase 2 extended coverage to a much wider population, including staff licensed or registered for securities, insurance or MPF activities.
provisions.counselNote: References carry personal data and defamation risk; set a defensible process for recording conduct information and responding to requests.

provisions.title: Limits on exposures to connected parties
provisions.summary: Connected-party exposure limits, formerly in Part XV of the Banking Ordinance, have sat in Part 8 of the BELR since 1 July 2019; breach of the rule 87 limits is a notifiable event. HKMA systems and controls expectations are in SPM CR-G-9 (Exposures to Connected Parties). Connected parties broadly include directors, controllers, group companies and persons related to them.
provisions.counselNote: A tech-parented bank has dense intra-group dealings; flag group entities and key people in exposure systems, keep terms no more favourable than arm's length, and treat a limit breach as an immediate reporting issue.

checklist: Map the full ownership chain to ultimate owners and identify everyone who is, or could become, a minority, majority or indirect controller.
Insert s.70 consent as a condition precedent, with realistic long-stop dates, in any transaction affecting group shareholdings, including parent-level fundraisings and restructurings.
Maintain a register of s.71 consents and s.72B notifications, with a succession timetable that allows for HKMA processing time.
Benchmark board and committee composition and charters against CG-1 (V.4, August 2025).
Review the remuneration policy and sales incentive schemes against CG-5 and the Bank Culture Reform circulars.
Embed MRC Phase 2 steps into recruitment and leaver workflows, with PDPO-compliant record-keeping.
Inventory intra-group arrangements (cloud, data, payments, marketing, shared staff) and test them against connected-party limits, CR-G-9 and outsourcing requirements.
Keep controllers' letters of comfort current, brief the parent on its continuing obligations as a controller, and assess how the holding company regime in the 2026 Bill would affect the group.
itAngle: Model the group as a graph: controller status depends on voting power aggregated through holding chains and associates, much like computing effective permissions through nested groups in an identity and access system.

Accountability maps (s.72B managers and regulated-activity responsibilities) should line up with system ownership; each critical platform should have a named, notified individual, and RACI or CMDB ownership data are useful evidence.
MRC and fit and proper records are personal data: design retention, access control and data-correction processes under the PDPO.
Technology services from a tech parent are both a connected-party and an outsourcing issue; feed the outsourcing register and the connected-exposure system from one source of truth.
virtualBankNotes: Where the bank is not majority-owned by a supervised bank or financial institution, the HKMA expects a Hong Kong intermediate holding company; it and the ultimate parent will typically be controllers needing s.70 consent, the HKMA attaches supervisory conditions to that consent, and letters of comfort are expected. The 2026 Bill would allow direct supervision of designated holding companies.
Tech-group parents often have founders, venture funds and public shareholders upstream; changes in that cap table are a common source of unexpected controller approvals.
Executives shared with or seconded from the parent need s.71 consent or s.72B notification in their bank role, plus conflicts management under CG-1.
pitfalls: Looking only at the bank's own share register, when controller status is tested through the ownership chain and with associates.
Announcing or completing an appointment before the MA's s.71 consent is given.
Running regulated-activity accountability mapping and s.72B notifications as separate exercises, leaving gaps the HKMA will notice.
Assuming intra-group arrangements are exempt because they are within the family; connected-party limits and arm's-length expectations still apply.

glossary.definition: A person who, alone or with associates, is entitled to exercise or control 10% or more, but not more than 50%, of the voting power at general meetings of an AI or of a company of which it is a subsidiary.
A person who, alone or with associates, is entitled to exercise or control more than 50% of that voting power.
A person in accordance with whose directions or instructions the directors of an AI, or of its holding company, are accustomed to act.

Under the Banking Ordinance, an individual appointed by an AI to be principally responsible, alone or jointly, for the conduct of particular affairs or business; appointments are notified to the MA under s.72B.
The SFC's term for individuals principally responsible for core functions of a licensed corporation; the HKMA applies a parallel accountability approach to registered institutions.
A letter from a controller to the HKMA committing to provide capital and/or liquidity support to the AI if needed.
Independent non-executive director. CG-1 sets expectations for the number, independence and expertise of INEDs on the boards of locally incorporated AIs.
An HKMA-endorsed industry scheme requiring AIs to obtain and give conduct-related references when hiring into covered roles, to stop misconduct following people between banks.

title: Capital & liquidity
oneLiner: Capital and liquidity ratios decide whether the bank can grow, pay dividends or stay licensed; counsel owns the legal plumbing.
overview: Prudential regulation asks two questions: can the bank absorb losses, and can it pay depositors on demand? Capital is the loss-absorbing layer, measured as a percentage of [[risk-weighted assets|RWA]], with [[CET1]] as the highest-quality tier. Liquidity is the cash-flow layer: enough liquid assets and stable funding to survive outflows. Hong Kong implements the Basel framework mainly through rules made under the Banking Ordinance (Cap. 155): the Banking (Capital) Rules (Cap. 155L), Banking (Liquidity) Rules (Cap. 155Q), Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (Cap. 155S) and Banking (Disclosure) Rules (Cap. 155M), supplemented by Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) modules. The rules supply the formulae; the HKMA's supervisory review ([[Pillar 2]]) adds bank-specific requirements. Counsel rarely runs the numbers, but owns the legal architecture around them: board approvals, capital instruments, parent support, limits on distributions and the accuracy of what is reported.
deepDive:
Think of capital as a stack of thresholds. The Banking (Capital) Rules set minimums of 4.5% CET1, 6% Tier 1 and 8% total capital. Above these sit buffers: a 2.5% [[capital conservation buffer]], a [[countercyclical capital buffer]] (CCyB) weighted by where the bank's private-sector credit exposures are located (the HKMA cut Hong Kong's rate to 0.5% in October 2024), and, for D-SIBs only, a higher loss absorbency surcharge. Using a buffer is not a breach, but it triggers automatic limits on distributions: dividends, buybacks, discretionary bonuses and AT1 coupons. A 3% [[leverage ratio]], which ignores risk weights, acts as a backstop.

The MA can raise an individual bank's minimums under s.97F of the Banking Ordinance, after giving it a chance to make representations. This is how the Pillar 2A add-on from the supervisory review under SPM CA-G-5 becomes legally binding. The bank's real floor is therefore higher than the published Basel figures, and it is usually confidential.

Most of the Basel III final reform package took effect on 1 January 2025: revised credit and operational risk, and an [[output floor]] that rises in stages to 72.5%. The market risk and CVA changes followed their own HKMA timetable, so confirm which apply to the bank. For a bank on standardised approaches the floor rarely bites. The revised risk weights and the new operational risk charge matter more.

Liquidity uses two tiers. Category 1 institutions, designated by the MA, must meet the LCR and NSFR. All other AIs are category 2 and must meet a 25% [[LMR]]; category 2A institutions must also meet a 75% core funding ratio. The Exposure Limits Rules cap exposure to any counterparty group at 25% of Tier 1 and also govern exposures to connected parties, including the bank's own shareholders.

For a loss-making digital bank, the key judgements concern runway. Operating losses reduce CET1 directly. Deferred tax assets arising from tax losses are deducted, and so is capitalised software held as an intangible, so accounting equity overstates regulatory capital. The capital plan should show when ratios will reach the board's internal trigger, which sits above the Pillar 2A floor plus buffers. Parent injections should be approved in advance and documented. Dividends are not an option until accumulated losses have been cleared, because company law allows distributions only out of distributable profits (Cap. 622, Part 6).

provisions.ref: Capital adequacy ratios, buffers and leverage ratio
provisions.title: Minimum capital ratios and buffers
provisions.summary: The Rules set the minimum CET1 (4.5%), Tier 1 (6%) and total capital (8%) ratios and define what counts as capital and which deductions apply. They also set the capital conservation, countercyclical and D-SIB buffers, which carry distribution constraints, and a minimum leverage ratio of 3%.
provisions.counselNote: The legal definition of eligible capital decides whether a parent injection counts as CET1. Distribution constraints also limit dividends and discretionary bonuses before any formal breach.

provisions.title: MA's power to vary capital requirements for a particular AI
provisions.summary: Allows the MA to vary capital requirement rules for a particular AI, including raising its minimum capital adequacy ratios, where it is satisfied on reasonable grounds that this is prudent. The AI may make representations before the variation takes effect.
provisions.counselNote: This is the legal route for Pillar 2A add-ons. Treat a proposed variation as a decision with due-process rights, and keep the resulting minimums in a controlled, confidential register.

provisions.title: Basel III final reform package
provisions.summary: Amends Cap. 155L to implement the revised credit risk, operational risk, market risk (FRTB) and CVA risk frameworks and the output floor. Following LegCo negative vetting in early 2024, a commencement notice gazetted in October 2024 brought them into force on 1 January 2025. The HKMA set a separate timetable for the market risk and CVA requirements; confirm which are in force for the bank.
provisions.counselNote: Any capital plan, board paper or pricing model from before 2025 rests on the old risk weights. Ask Finance to confirm that projections and RWA engines reflect the amended Rules.

provisions.title: Liquidity ratios
provisions.summary: Category 1 institutions, designated by the MA, must keep the LCR and NSFR at or above 100%. Category 2 institutions must meet a 25% Liquidity Maintenance Ratio, and category 2A institutions must also meet a 75% Core Funding Ratio. SPM LM-1 gives the detailed supervisory guidance.
provisions.counselNote: Confirm the bank's designated category in writing. Treat a ratio breach as a notification event with an escalation path to the board and the HKMA.

provisions.title: Large exposure limit and connected exposures
provisions.summary: Limits an AI's exposure to any single counterparty or linked counterparty group to 25% of Tier 1 capital, and separately controls exposures to connected parties. The Rules came into force on 1 July 2019 and took full effect after a six-month grace period. SPM CR-G-8 treats exposures at or above 10% of Tier 1 as large exposures.
provisions.counselNote: Intra-group placements, guarantees and service prepayments to the parent are exposures to connected parties, so check them before signing. Placing surplus deposits with a few banks can also reach the 25% limit.

provisions.title: Public regulatory disclosures
provisions.summary: Requires AIs to publish standardised information on capital, RWA, leverage, liquidity and risk management, using HKMA templates and at prescribed frequencies.
provisions.counselNote: Pillar 3 disclosures are public statements. They need the same verification and sign-off discipline as financial statements, and must be consistent with what the bank tells investors and customers.

provisions.title: Supervisory review process (Pillar 2)
provisions.summary: A statutory guideline issued under s.7(3) of the Banking Ordinance. It sets out how the HKMA assesses each AI's capital adequacy assessment process (CAAP/ICAAP) and sets Pillar 2 requirements, including expectations on stress testing within the CAAP.
provisions.counselNote: The ICAAP is a board document. Make sure the board can show it challenged the document rather than simply receiving it.

provisions.title: Stress-testing
provisions.summary: A guidance note, revised in 2012 to reflect Basel stress-testing principles, on how AIs should design, govern and use stress tests. The HKMA applies it proportionately to the scale and complexity of the AI.
provisions.counselNote: Stress-test outputs feed capital planning, recovery triggers and exit-plan triggers. Make sure the scenarios include a fast digital deposit run and a failure of parent support.

provisions.title: Interest rate risk in the banking book
provisions.summary: Sets out HKMA expectations for measuring, managing and reporting interest rate risk on non-trading positions, broadly in line with the Basel IRRBB standards.
provisions.counselNote: A bank that wins deposits by pricing promotions and then holds fixed-rate assets is exposed to interest rate risk. Product terms on repricing and early withdrawal are legal levers that affect this risk.

provisions.title: Limits on distributions inside the buffers
provisions.summary: When a bank's CET1 ratio falls into its buffer range (capital conservation, countercyclical and any D-SIB buffer), the Rules cap distributions such as dividends, discretionary bonuses and AT1 coupons at a maximum distributable amount until the buffers are rebuilt.
provisions.counselNote: Separately, company law allows dividends only out of distributable profits (Companies Ordinance, Cap. 622, Part 6), so a start-up bank with accumulated losses cannot pay any. Check both tests before approving a distribution.

checklist: Obtain the bank's current Pillar 2A / s.97F capital notice, its liquidity category designation and the board-approved internal trigger levels, and hold them in a controlled register.

Build a capital-runway calendar with Finance: monthly CET1 projections against the board trigger, plus the lead time for a parent injection (board and shareholder resolutions, allotment and any HKMA engagement).
Review parent support documents (letter of comfort, capital support agreement) and confirm that planned injections will qualify as CET1.
Screen every intra-group arrangement (service fees, guarantees, deposits with or loans to group companies) against the connected-exposure rules and arm's-length terms before signing.
Embed legal review in regulatory reporting governance: attestations, treatment of manual adjustments, and a protocol for notifying the HKMA of errors and restating returns.
Test every proposed distribution (dividends, discretionary bonuses, AT1 coupons) against the buffer stack (Cap. 155L ss.3F–3K) and the Companies Ordinance (Cap. 622) distributable-profits rule.
Brief the board each year on the ICAAP, stress-test results and capital and liquidity triggers, and make sure the minutes record real challenge.
Track HKMA consultations and amendments to Cap. 155L, 155Q and 155S, and map each change to a system change request and owner.
itAngle: The capital and RWA engine is effectively a rules engine that encodes Cap. 155L. Treat each rule amendment like a release: trace each provision to calculation logic, then to a test case, then to the cell in the return. Counsel can own the interpretation log for that release.

Regulatory returns are legal statements to the regulator. Insist on documented data lineage from the core ledger to each return, automated reconciliations and four-eyes control over manual overrides, in line with BCBS 239 data-aggregation principles.
Large-exposure and connected-exposure monitoring is an entity-resolution problem. Grouping counterparties correctly needs reliable data on corporate hierarchies and control.
Deposits can leave at app speed over FPS, 24x7. Liquidity monitoring and stress scenarios should model weekend and intraday outflows at digital run velocity, not branch-era assumptions.
Capitalised software is generally deducted from CET1 as an intangible asset, so build, buy or SaaS decisions have regulatory capital consequences as well as accounting ones.
virtualBankNotes: A digital bank is a licensed bank and is subject to the same capital, liquidity and exposure rules. There is no lighter prudential regime, and the HK$300 million minimum paid-up capital for licensed banks applies.
Start-up losses erode CET1 every month. The HKMA expects shareholders to stand behind the bank, and its digital bank guidance cautions against aggressive growth funded by sustained losses.
Digital banks are typically category 2 institutions for liquidity (LMR-based) unless the MA designates otherwise. Confirm the bank's actual designation.
A deposit-rich, loan-light balance sheet pushes surplus funds into interbank placements and securities. Concentration there can reach large-exposure limits.
pitfalls: Treating accounting equity as regulatory capital, and overlooking CET1 deductions for deferred tax assets on tax losses and for capitalised software and other intangibles.
Assuming the headline Basel minimums plus buffers are the binding floor, when the confidential Pillar 2A add-on and board triggers sit higher.
Relying on informal parent support (comfort letters, emails) as if it were capital that will arrive on time in a crisis.
Letting finance teams fix return errors quietly instead of following a defined notification and restatement process with the HKMA.

glossary.definition: Common Equity Tier 1: ordinary shares, share premium, retained earnings and disclosed reserves, less regulatory deductions such as intangibles and certain deferred tax assets. It is the highest-quality capital and absorbs losses first.
Risk-weighted assets: the bank's exposures weighted for credit, market, operational and CVA risk under the Capital Rules. RWA is the denominator of the capital ratios.
The supervisory review layer, in which the HKMA assesses risks not fully captured by the Pillar 1 formulae and sets bank-specific add-ons (a binding Pillar 2A minimum and a Pillar 2B buffer).
A 2.5% of RWA layer of CET1 held above the minimum. If the bank's capital falls into it, automatic restrictions on distributions apply.

A time-varying CET1 buffer that authorities set for each jurisdiction according to credit conditions. A bank's applicable rate is the weighted average of the rates where its private-sector credit exposures sit.
A Basel III limit on the benefit of internal models: total RWA cannot fall below a set percentage (72.5% when fully phased in) of RWA calculated under the standardised approaches.

Liquidity Maintenance Ratio: Hong Kong's local liquidity metric for category 2 institutions, comparing liquefiable assets with qualifying short-term liabilities. The minimum is 25%, measured as a monthly average.
Tier 1 capital divided by an unweighted measure of on- and off-balance-sheet exposures. The minimum is 3%, as a backstop to risk-based ratios.

title: Technology & outsourcing
oneLiner: For a digital bank, technology and vendor failures are banking failures; HKMA expects them governed, contracted and reported.
overview: For a bank with no branches, technology is the bank: accounts, payments and every customer interaction run on code, cloud services and third-party vendors. The Banking Ordinance says little about IT directly. The rules that actually apply sit in the HKMA's [[Supervisory Policy Manual]] and circulars: TM-G-1 (technology risk), TM-E-1 (e-banking), SA-2 (outsourcing), OR-1, OR-2 and TM-G-2 (operational risk, resilience and continuity), and the [[C-RAF]] cyber assessment. Since 1 January 2026, Cap. 653 has added statutory cyber duties for designated [[critical infrastructure operators|critical infrastructure operator]], and PDPO DPP4 governs personal data security throughout. The rules exist because operational failure at a bank harms depositors and payment systems quickly. Counsel's job is to turn them into contracts, governance records, incident playbooks and accurate, timely notifications to the regulator.
deepDive:
Start with status. The SPM mixes [[statutory guidelines|statutory guideline]] issued under s.7(3) of the Banking Ordinance (TM-E-1 since its October 2024 revision) with non-statutory guidance notes (TM-G-1, which dates from 2003, and OR-2). In practice the difference is small: the HKMA tests whether the bank continues to meet the Seventh Schedule minimum criteria, including adequate systems of control, against all of them. Persistent shortfalls feed into CAMEL ratings and, ultimately, s.52 directions. Treat every 'should' as an expectation: meet it, or depart from it on a documented basis the board can see.

Outsourcing is where counsel earns their keep. SA-2 (2001) expects the bank to discuss any [[material outsourcing]], or a significant change to one, with the HKMA in advance. Agreements should give the HKMA and auditors access and inspection rights, protect customer data, control sub-contracting and support contingency and exit. Offshore processing must not impede HKMA access to data. For cloud, read SA-2 with the Practice Guide on Cloud Adoption (8 January 2026), reported to replace the 2022 cloud guidance. Hyperscalers' standard terms rarely deliver all of this without a financial-services addendum.

OR-2 (May 2022) implements the Basel operational resilience principles. The bank must identify its [[critical operations|critical operation]], set a [[tolerance for disruption]] for each, map its people, technology and third-party dependencies, and test against severe but plausible scenarios. The 31 May 2026 deadline has passed; the HKMA's June 2026 letter reports that all AIs met it and expects resilience to be sustained as business as usual. Examiners ask for board approvals and test evidence, not policies.

Incident reporting runs on parallel tracks. The HKMA expects immediate notice of significant incidents with whatever facts are available, and waiting for root cause can itself draw a finding. If the bank has been designated under Cap. 653, statutory deadlines for notifying the Commissioner also apply: 12 hours for serious incidents, 48 hours for others, then a written report within 14 days. PDPO, police and customer communications each follow their own rules. Build one triage tree that starts every clock at once.

TM-E-1 and the HKMA's 2025 e-banking security measures make in-app [[bound device]] authentication the default for mobile app users instead of SMS OTP. The August 2024 GenAI circular applies governance, fairness, transparency and privacy principles to customer-facing AI.

provisions.title: General Principles for Technology Risk Management
provisions.summary: Non-statutory guidance note (V.1, 24 June 2003) setting baseline expectations for technology risk governance, information security, system development and change management, IT operations and management of technology service providers.
provisions.counselNote: This is the baseline the HKMA uses to judge whether IT controls are 'adequate'. It is old, so the HKMA reads it alongside later modules and circulars, and you should too when advising on control gaps.

provisions.title: Outsourcing
provisions.summary: Sets HKMA expectations for outsourcing (dated 28 December 2001): board accountability, risk assessment and due diligence, written agreements, confidentiality of customer data, monitoring and control, contingency planning, HKMA access, and additional issues for overseas outsourcing. AIs should discuss plans for material outsourcing, or significant changes to its scope, with the HKMA before proceeding.
provisions.counselNote: This is the source of the HKMA's required clauses in vendor contracts, in particular supervisory inspection and access rights. For a digital bank most core vendors will be material, so the HKMA pre-consultation must be built into procurement timelines.

provisions.title: Operational Resilience
provisions.summary: Non-statutory guidance note issued on 31 May 2022, together with a revised TM-G-2 on business continuity planning, to implement the Basel Committee's March 2021 Principles for Operational Resilience; a revised OR-1 on operational risk management followed on 25 July 2022. AIs were to develop their operational resilience framework by 31 May 2023 and be operationally resilient by 31 May 2026.
provisions.counselNote: The deadline has passed. The HKMA's letter 'Operational Resilience: Sustaining and Uplifting' (June 2026) reports that, on its survey, all AIs met it, and shifts the focus to sustaining and improving resilience. Expect examiners to test board ownership of critical operations, tolerances, dependency mapping (including vendors) and scenario testing.

provisions.title: Risk Management of E-banking
provisions.summary: Revised version (V.4, 25 October 2024), issued as a statutory guideline under s.7(3) of the Banking Ordinance; earlier versions were non-statutory guidance notes. It extends the module to controls over payment card transactions, consolidates e-banking security measures previously spread across supervisory documents (including the 2016 circular on internet banking security controls), and is more principle-based.
provisions.counselNote: This is the core rulebook for a digital-only bank's customer channels, covering authentication, fraud monitoring and mobile app security. The HKMA's April 2025 'E-Banking Security ABC' measures build on it: 'Authenticate in-App' makes bound-device authentication the default for mobile app users instead of SMS OTP (due by Q4 2025), and an August 2025 letter extended the package to 'ABCD' by adding deepfake detection.

provisions.title: Security of personal data
provisions.summary: Requires data users to take all practicable steps to protect personal data against unauthorised or accidental access, processing, erasure, loss or use. Where a data processor is engaged, the data user must adopt contractual or other means to secure equivalent protection.
provisions.counselNote: DPP4(2) is the statutory basis for data-processor security clauses in every outsourcing contract. Use it together with SA-2's customer-confidentiality expectations and the bank's common-law duty of confidentiality.

provisions.instrument: Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance (Cap. 653)
provisions.title: Critical infrastructure cybersecurity duties
provisions.summary: In force from 1 January 2026. Operators designated as critical infrastructure operators, including in the banking and financial services sector, bear three categories of duties for their designated critical computer systems: organisational, preventive (such as annual risk assessments and two-yearly audits), and incident reporting and response. Serious incidents must be notified to the Commissioner of Critical Infrastructure (Computer-system Security) within 12 hours of becoming aware, others within 48 hours, followed by a written report within 14 days. The HKMA is the designated authority for the banking and financial services sector and administers the organisational and preventive obligations of operators in that sector.
provisions.counselNote: Designation is by written notice, so confirm whether the bank or any of its systems has been designated. If it has, statutory deadlines and audit and risk-assessment cycles apply on top of HKMA expectations; read the HKMA's Code of Practice for designated AIs (2 June 2026) with the Ordinance. An HKMA–Commissioner MoU dated 29 May 2026 coordinates the two regulators.

provisions.instrument: HKMA circular: Incident response and management procedures
provisions.title: Reporting significant incidents to the HKMA
provisions.summary: Reminds AIs to maintain an effective capability to respond to significant incidents and to notify the HKMA immediately on becoming aware of one, without waiting until the problem has been fixed. AIs should also notify affected customers and consider a public announcement where the situation warrants. Later HKMA letters, such as the 12 August 2014 circular on disruptions of critical banking services, point back to it.
provisions.counselNote: The HKMA has not published a list of notifiable incidents, so the bank must judge significance itself. Write internal significance criteria, have management endorse them and apply them consistently, because those criteria are what examiners will test.

provisions.instrument: HKMA Practice Guide on Cloud Adoption
provisions.title: Cloud adoption expectations
provisions.summary: Combines high-level principles drawn from relevant SPM modules with good practices the HKMA has observed in supervision, following a lifecycle approach. It expands the cloud-related domains covered from four to eight and is reported to supersede the HKMA's 2022 cloud computing guidance.
provisions.counselNote: Read it with SA-2 on every cloud deal. The HKMA notes that cloud projects make up about 80% of reportable technology outsourcing initiatives, so expect scrutiny of concentration risk, security, resilience and exit.

provisions.title: C-RAF and CFI 2.0
provisions.summary: CFI 2.0, effective 1 January 2021 and implemented in phases, keeps three pillars: the Cyber Resilience Assessment Framework (inherent risk assessment, maturity assessment and intelligence-led attack simulation testing), a Professional Development Programme, and the Cyber Intelligence Sharing Platform. The 2.0 review streamlined the C-RAF assessment process and refreshed its control principles, which industry summaries say now reflect current incident response and recovery practice.
provisions.counselNote: C-RAF assessments and attack-simulation findings are supervisory deliverables. Agree confidentiality and report-handling terms with testers, and assume the HKMA will read remediation plans.

provisions.instrument: HKMA circular: Consumer Protection in respect of Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
provisions.title: GenAI in customer-facing applications
provisions.summary: Applies the four consumer-protection principles from the HKMA's 5 November 2019 big data analytics and AI circular (governance and accountability, fairness, transparency and disclosure, data privacy and protection) to customer-facing GenAI use, with additional GenAI-specific expectations.
provisions.counselNote: Before any chatbot, robo-advice or AI marketing goes live, check board and senior management accountability, fairness testing, and disclosure to customers. The HKMA–Cyberport GenA.I. Sandbox (launched 13 August 2024, expanded in 2026 as the cross-regulator GenA.I. Sandbox++) provides supervisory feedback but no legal exemption.

checklist: Build and maintain an outsourcing register that flags material arrangements, cloud workloads, data locations and sub-contractors, and reconcile it against what has been discussed with the HKMA.
